item.title: Sneezes Shouldn't Stand Between You and Puppy Love
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • The real trigger for dog allergies isn't just fur — it's the protein found in dander and in saliva that can travel through the environment on loose hair and settle on furniture, clothes, and carpets
  • No dog breed is completely hypoallergenic, but low-shedding and hairless breeds produce fewer airborne allergens, making them a more manageable option for people with mild to moderate allergies
  • Popular hypoallergenic breeds include Poodles, Bichon Frise, Yorkshire Terriers, Maltese, Shih Tzus, Schnauzers, Portuguese Water Dogs, Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers, and the growing family of doodle mixes
  • Lesser-known options like the Xoloitzcuintli, Peruvian Inca Orchid, Coton de Tulear, Bedlington Terrier, Lagotto Romagnolo, and Afghan Hound offer more variety for allergy-prone families willing to search a little harder
  • Adopt A Pet Month in October is a great reminder that hypoallergenic dogs regularly turn up in breed-specific rescues, and adopting an adult means fewer surprises about coat, dander, and temperament

You've wanted a dog for as long as you can remember. But every time you visit a friend's place with a shedding pup, you end up sneezing, itching, and wondering if the whole dream is off the table. Maybe your kid has been begging for a puppy, maybe you've been telling yourself “Someday" for years….

The good news is that dog ownership is not off the table for people with allergies. It just requires being a little more thoughtful about which dog joins the family. Certain breeds shed less, produce less dander, and are more commonly tolerated by allergy-prone people. And plenty of them end up in rescues, waiting for the right home.

What's Really Causing Your Sneezing?

Most people assume dog fur is the enemy. It's not — at least not directly. The actual culprit is dander, which are tiny flakes of skin that all dogs shed. Add in proteins found in a dog's saliva from them grooming themselves and you have the trigger of most allergic reactions. Fur is just the vehicle that carries those proteins around your house, from the couch to your clothes to the carpet and through the air.1,2

This is why heavy shedders spread more allergens through the environment — every loose hair becomes a delivery system. It is also why low-shedding breeds tend to be easier for people with allergies. Less shedding means fewer airborne allergens, less accumulation on surfaces, and fewer sneezes. Common symptoms include sneezing, runny nose, itchy eyes, wheezing, coughing, and skin rashes.

What Hypoallergenic Really Means

The truth is that no dog is 100% hypoallergenic. Every dog produces allergens through their skin dander and in their saliva - even hairless breeds. What some breeds do offer is a lower allergen load and less shedding, which together can make life much easier for allergy sufferers as less hair means that fewer airborne allergenic particles are present.3,4

Certain breeds have hair that keeps growing (more like human hair) rather than fur and do not shed. Others have tightly curled coats that trap dander before it can spread through the air. Some are simply hairless. Any of these can be a good fit if your allergic reactions are mild to moderate.

Popular and Widely Available

Some hypoallergenic breeds have become household names for good reason — their low allergy tendency is well known and they are widely available through breeders and from breed specific rescues. If you're just starting your search, these are the breeds that most people find first. Be aware that any non-shedding breed will need professional grooming every six to eight weeks to trim their hair and keep their coat manageable. t5,6

  • Poodle — Probably the best-known hypoallergenic breed. Their dense, curly coats trap dander and shed minimally. Highly intelligent and trainable. They come in three sizes — standard, miniature, and toy — so you can select which one suits your home.
  • Bichon Frise — Small, friendly, with a fluffy curly coat. Very affectionate, playful with kids, and adaptable.
  • Yorkshire Terrier — A toy breed with silky, human-like hair. It fits in apartments and large homes alike. Confident and lively personality.
  • Maltese — Long, silky white hair that doesn't shed much. Playful and affectionate.
  • Shih Tzu — Thick coat, friendly temperament, ancient companion breed. Their flat face means keeping an eye on breathing and temperature.
  • Schnauzer (Miniature, Standard, and Giant) All three sizes are low-shedding with wiry double coats. They are smart, alert, and adaptable to different living situations.
  • Portuguese Water Dog — A medium-sized athletic breed. Loves water, and needs lots of exercise.
  • Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier — Medium-sized Terrier with a silky, low-shedding coat. Active and family-oriented.
  • Doodle mixes — Poodles that have been crossed with various breeds to make them hypoallergenic. These may include Labradoodles, Goldendoodles, and many more. Coats vary, but many are low-shedding. Increasingly common in breed specific rescues.

Lesser-Known Breeds That Are Worth Considering

If the popular breeds aren't quite the right fit, or you want something a little more unique, there's a second tier of hypoallergenic dogs that fly under most people's radar. These breeds may take more searching to find, but they can be exactly what an allergy sufferer needs:7,8

  • Kerry Blue Terrier — Energetic and loyal with a non-shedding, wavy coat. Some may have a strong temperament so working with the breeder to find the right pup for your family is recommended.
  • Chinese Crested — Comes in hairless and powderpuff varieties, which are both hypoallergenic. The hairless version has minimal dander but needs skin protection from the sun.
  • American Hairless Terrier — Friendly, intelligent, and great for people with severe allergies. Low maintenance grooming needs.
  • Xoloitzcuintli — An ancient Mexican breed available in three sizes and both hairless and coated varieties. Calm, loyal, and rare.
  • Peruvian Inca Orchid — A mostly hairless breed native to Peru. Comes in three sizes and is quite rare in the U.S.
  • Coton de Tulear — A small, easygoing dog from Madagascar with a cotton-soft coat. Great with kids and other pets.
  • Bedlington Terrier — Small, curly-coated, and famously lamb-like in appearance with the right haircut.
  • Afghan Hound — striking, long, silky coat that surprisingly sheds very little. Dignified and independent.
  • Lagotto Romagnolo — An Italian water dog with a curly, woolly coat. Friendly, energetic, and good with families.
  • Irish Water Spaniel — The clown of the spaniel family. Curly liver-brown coat, highly trainable, and needs daily exercise.

Yes, You Can Still Adopt — Even with Allergies

October is Adopt a Pet Month, and it's the perfect time to remember that allergy-friendly dogs aren't only found through breeders. Rescue organizations across the country have hypoallergenic breeds waiting for homes right now. Poodles, Bichons, Yorkies, Maltese, Schnauzers, Shih Tzus, and every kind of doodle mix may be available through rescues. . Breed-specific rescues exist for almost every hypoallergenic breed on that list.

If you're specifically looking for a low-shedding dog due to allergies, tell the rescue exactly that. Many will help match you with a dog whose coat type and temperament fit your household. Be aware that shelters and rescues may not always know the true breed of a mixed dog and may advertise that it is hypoallergenic or a “doodle” mix when it may not be to help them get adopted. Meeting the dog in person first — spending real time with them, ideally over a couple of visits — is the best way to gauge how your allergies will react before you commit to adopting. Some rescues offer trial adoption periods for exactly this reason.

Adopting rather than shopping means you're giving a home to a dog who needs one, and often adult dogs come with the benefit of known personalities, prior house training, and less of the surprise factor that puppies bring. With an adult dog, what you see is largely what you get — coat type is fully developed, temperament is settled, and any dander reactions you have during a visit are a realistic preview of daily life.

If allergies are the reason you have been holding back, this is your chance to take one more look. Speak with a rescue group to see if they have a short term fostering program available so that you can spend time with the prospective pup in your home to see how your allergies react before making a long term a commitment.

Making It Work at Home

Choosing a low-shedding breed is only half of the equation. How you set up your home matters just as much. A few practical steps that make a real difference:

  • Groom frequently — Regular brushing (weekly at minimum) and bathing every four to eight weeks removes loose dander before it spreads. A professional groomer is worth the investment for non-shedding and curly coated breeds to prevent their coats from growing too long and becoming matted.
  • Use a HEPA air filter — These trap airborne pet allergens and are especially useful in bedrooms and shared living spaces.
  • Vacuum often — A vacuum with a HEPA filter picks up dander from carpets, upholstery, and pet areas. Do it more often than you think you need to.
  • Wash bedding weekly — Your dog's bed, blankets, and any covers they hang out on should be laundered on a regular schedule.
  • Create allergy-free zones — Keeping your bedroom pet-free gives your immune system a break overnight.
  • Remove heavy carpets and drapes where possible — Fabric surfaces hold onto dander. Hard flooring is easier to keep clean.
  • Wipe your dog down — A quick wipe with damp cloth after outdoor time removes allergens from the coat.
  • Keep your own hygiene in mind — Wash your hands after handling your dog and avoid touching your face.

Test the Waters First

Before committing to a specific dog or breed, spend some real time around them. Ask friends who have the breed if you can visit. Attend breed-specific meetups or dog shows. Volunteer at a local rescue that has hypoallergenic dogs. Sit with them, pet them, and see how you react and bond with them.

Talk to your allergist or healthcare provider too. They can help you understand the severity of your allergies, suggest management strategies, and give you a clearer sense of what's realistic for your situation. Some allergy sufferers do so well with immunotherapy over time that a dog they once couldn't tolerate becomes perfectly manageable.9,10

Don’t Be Afraid to Make Room for a Furry Friend

Allergies used to be treated as a hard stop for anyone dreaming of a dog. They're not anymore. With the right breed, the right household habits, and a little conversation with your doctor, plenty of people with mild to moderate dog allergies happily share their homes with a furry family member. It just takes matching the right dog to your specific situation — and being realistic that no dog is perfectly allergen-free.

If you've been holding back because of allergies, contact your local rescue and ask about the hypoallergenic dogs they have, and the ones coming in. Spend time with them before adopting. There's a very good chance the dog who's been waiting for you is closer than you think — and there's no reason a few sneezes should stand between the two of you.

Sources and References

  • 1,9 Baz Allergy, Asthma, and Sinus Center, The Best Dog Breeds for Allergy Sufferers
  • 2,3,6,8 American Kennel Club, August 17, 2026
  • 4,5,7,10 PetMD, February 9, 2026

item.title: Working Dogs ‘Talk’ with the Help of Wearable Computers
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Technology known as FIDO, or Facilitating Interactions for Dogs with Occupations, aims to improve communication between humans and their canine partners
  • The FIDO team has developed wearable technology that is integrated into assistance dog vests in the form of sensors
  • Dogs are then trained to activate the sensors (by biting, tugging or using nose gestures) to communicate different messages or even call for help
  • In training sessions, a border collie named Sky learned to activate the sensors correctly in under 30 seconds, while the longest time among other dogs was about 30 minutes
  • FIDO’s primary goal is to serve working dogs, and it’s unclear whether a version for companion pets will be produced

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published April 20, 2017.

You can probably guess a lot of what your dog is trying to tell you just by gazing into her eyes or observing the wagging of her tail. But have you ever wished your dog could actually talk?

Technology known as FIDO, or Facilitating Interactions for Dogs with Occupations, may make this a reality, at least for service dogs, search-and-rescue dogs and police dogs.

FIDO, an ongoing research project at Georgia Tech's Animal Computer Interaction Lab that was founded by associate professor Melody Moore Jackson, Ph.D., aims to improve communication between humans and their canine partners.

While working dogs can communicate a variety of sometimes life-saving messages to their handlers — from alerting a rescue team to a person's location in an avalanche to letting a hearing-impaired person know their doorbell is ringing — they are limited in how much they can "say."

The FIDO team has developed wearable technology that is integrated into assistance dog vests in the form of sensors. Dogs are then trained to activate the sensors (by biting, tugging or using nose gestures) to communicate different messages.

In 2014, the researchers wrote, "We were able to demonstrate that it is possible to create wearable sensors that dogs can reliably activate on command and to determine cognitive and physical factors that affect dogs' success with body-worn interaction technology,"1 and their accomplishments have only continued since.

Technology Allows Dogs to Communicate Life-Saving Messages

In the CBS News video above, you can watch as Jackson works with a border collie named Sky, who has learned to tap certain sensors in response to words like "help" or the sound of a fire alarm.

Upon hearing that her owner may be having a medical emergency or needs to be alerted of a fire alarm, Sky activates the appropriate sensors, on her FIDO vest or a touch screen, to get her message across.

The messages, in turn, may be sent via text message to her owner or another family member or used to dial 911 and communicate a person's location.

In training sessions, Jackson said Sky learned how to correctly activate the sensors in under 30 seconds. Among other dogs, the longest it took was about 30 minutes — still an impressive feat.2

FIDO technology also allows dogs to pull a sensor on their vest that plays a recording such as, "My owner needs help, please follow me," which could be life-saving for someone with epilepsy, for example. It could be game-changing for police and search-and-rescue teams as well.

According to Karen B. London, Ph.D., certified applied animal behaviorist and certified professional dog trainer, in The Bark:3

"Although dogs are often trained to search for multiple types of drugs or explosives, they are limited in their ability to communicate the details of their finds to their handlers.
It can make a big difference to everyone's safety if the dog can let a handler know that the bomb is a stable type or an unstable one that needs careful handling. This vest can allow a dog to share more specific information.
This group developed a vest that allows a dog who has found anyone trapped after a natural disaster to activate a sensor with a message for that person to hear. The message lets the trapped individual know that help is on the way.
Work is underway to develop a vest that allows a dog to activate a sensor that sends GPS coordinates to a handler. This allows the handler to join the dog, who does not have to leave the person who has been found.
That could be lifesaving for a child who is hiding or for a person who is unable to move for whatever reason."

Will FIDO Be Available for Companion Animals?

Jackson, who created the FIDO device in partnership with colleague Thad Starner, Ph.D., an expert in wearable computers, said their primary goal is to make FIDO available to the working dogs who need it, and it's unclear whether they intend to produce a similar device that could be used for companion pets (with adequate training).

Others, however, have tried. In 2013, The Nordic Society for Invention and Discovery (NSID) claimed to be developing a device called "No More Woof" that would translate EEG signals from your dog's brain into human language through a speaker.

The crowdfunded device has not yet materialized, however, leaving contributors confused and angry.4 On the contrary, the FIDO device is the real thing in terms of helping working dogs communicate valuable details to their handlers.

In terms of figuring out what your pet dog is thinking, however (such as how she really feels about your pet cat or whether she prefers beef or chicken), for now you'll have to be content with observing her body language and other communicatory signs.

If you have a particular burning question to ask your dog and you're open-minded, you can also seek the help of a reputable animal communicator.

Sources and References

  • 1 Personal and Ubiquitous Computing 19(1):155 · October 2014
  • 2 CBS News January 14, 2016
  • 3 The Bark May 20, 2016
  • 4 IEEE Spectrum January 19, 2017

item.title: Have Those Floppy Ears Been Listening the Whole Time?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Research suggests dogs sense a difference between the verbal and emotional components of speech
  • Dogs appear to process emotional cues and meanings of words in different hemispheres of the brain, similar to humans
  • The average dog understands about 165 different words, although they may learn more if you train them to
  • Dogs also read posture, gestures and eye contact, and will follow your gaze much like a 6-month-old infant when you convey the intention to communicate
  • Dogs tend to wag their tails to the right when they see something pleasant and more to the left when they see something threatening

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published July 16, 2015.

When you speak to your dog, you probably have a sixth sense that he somehow understands what you’re saying. Dogs are intelligent creatures, after all, and they’ve been living with humans for tens of thousands of years.

The average dog understands about 165 different words, although they may learn more if you train them to.1 It’s known that dogs pay attention to the tone of human voices, the pitch and the rhythms in speech, but whether or not they pay attention to the meaning of the words was less clear — until now.

Researchers from the University of Sussex in England conducted a unique experiment to determine whether dogs listen to human words, with results that may not be too surprising for many dog owners.

Dogs Process Speech in Ways Similar to Humans

When listening to another person speak, humans tend to use the left hemisphere of their brain to process the verbal content and the right hemisphere to process the emotional content and characteristics of speech (such as whether it’s familiar or not). According to study author Victoria Ratcliffe:2

“Previous studies have shown that other mammals also have hemispheric biases when processing their own species’ vocalizations, but no one had ever looked at whether biases existed in domesticated animals in response to the different components of human speech.”

The study, which was published in the journal Current Biology,3 involved 250 dogs that heard the “come” command out of speakers on the right or left side of their heads. The command was played with varying inflections, emotional cues, in different languages, and even with gibberish in place of the words.

The researchers then recorded whether the dogs turned their heads toward the left or right speaker. A pattern emerged, with the dogs turning toward the right when they heard meaningful words and to the left when the command included just emotional cues.

The results suggest dogs are able to distinguish between meaningful and meaningless sounds. As reported by NPR:4

“The study also suggests that a dog's brain breaks up speech into two parts: the emotional cues and the meaning of the words. Then it processes these two components on opposite sides of the brain: emotional cues on the right, meaning of words on the left. (Yes, it's opposite to the way the dogs turned.)

That's a bit similar to how we humans process speech. We also break up speech into several parts, such as the meaning of the words, clues about the speaker and emotional cues.”

Although it appears dogs do sense a difference between the verbal and emotional components of speech, it’s still unclear to what extent they understand each.

Dogs Pay Attention to Your Non-Verbal Communication Too

When you communicate, it’s not only your words that matter. Your posture, gestures and eye contact also speak volumes, and your dog pays attention to these cues closely. Dogs will follow your gaze similarly to a 6-month-old infant, but only if you convey the intention of communication, which suggests they’re quite in-tune with your communicative signals.5

There are many theories as to why and how dogs developed such strong responsiveness to human communicative gestures. It could be that dogs spend more time around humans than other species, or that they quickly learned paying close attention might get them more rewards (like food). As reported in the journal Behavioral Processes:6

“Dogs are more skillful than a host of other species at tasks which require they respond to human communicative gestures in order to locate hidden food. Four basic interpretations for this proficiency surface from distilling the research findings.

One possibility is that dogs simply have more opportunity than other species to learn to be responsive to human social cues. A different analysis suggests that the domestication process provided an opening for dogs to apply general cognitive problem-solving skills to a novel social niche.

Some researchers go beyond this account and propose that dogs' co-evolution with humans equipped them with a theory of mind for social exchanges.

Finally, a more prudent approach suggests that sensitivity to the behaviors of both humans and conspecifics would be particularly advantageous for a social scavenger like the dog. A predisposition to attend to human actions allows for rapid early learning of the association between gestures and the availability of food.”

How Does Your Dog Communicate with You?

While humans use speech as a primary form of communicating, your dog may “talk” to you using different forms of communication — like tail movements. Dogs display submission by tucking their tails and lying on their backs. They display dominance by staring, raising their fur, and baring their teeth.

Further, dogs tend to wag their tails to the right side when they encounter something pleasant (like their owners). When they see something threatening, for example a strange dog exhibiting dominant behaviors, they wag more to the left side.7

Certain species of canines also use their eyes to communicate, and the fact that your dog will make direct eye contact with you may be one important feature that distinguishes him from wild dogs, or wolves. As written in Current Biology:8

“… we suggest that the key difference between dog and wolf behavior is the dogs' ability to look at the human's face.

Since looking behavior has an important function in initializing and maintaining communicative interaction in human communication systems, we suppose that by positive feedback processes (both evolutionary and ontogenetically) the readiness of dogs to look at the human face has lead to complex forms of dog-human communication that cannot be achieved in wolves even after extended socialization.”

Dogs are even known to respond in a unique way when a person cries. Many dogs approach crying people while displaying submissive behaviors, both of which suggest (but do not prove) some level of empathy.

It’s likely that ongoing research into the emotional lives and capabilities of dogs will continue to reveal their seemingly uncanny ability to understand us. And even if it doesn’t … simply looking into your dog’s eyes or having him sit loyally by your side after a hard day is proof enough for most dog owners.

  • 3 Current Biology December 15, 2014
  • 4 NPR November 28, 2014

  • 6 Behav Processes. 2009 Mar;80(3):325-33

item.title: 10 Telltale Signs of a Happy Dog, but This One Can Be Tricky
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Your dog is your BFF, but she’s also a different species, which is why there can be the occasional dog-to-human communication breakdown
  • If you can tell the difference relaxed, anxious and aggressive dog communication signals, you’ll be better able to speak your dog’s language
  • Happy dogs also display specific communication signals
  • Tail wagging and kisses don’t always signal happiness, since aggressive dogs can wag their tails as they attack and anxious dogs often kiss up a storm
  • Whale eye, yawning and lip licking are stress signals, not signs of a happy dog

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 14, 2020.

When you and your dog miscommunicate — either she doesn’t understand what you’re telling her or you can’t interpret her canine language — it can result in lots of missed signals, frustration, and can even damage the bond you share with her.

One example of the potential for misreading your dog is the common belief among humans that when a dog is wagging her tail or giving kisses, she’s happy. However, that’s not always the case. Aggressive dogs are known to wag their tails as they attack, and anxious pups often kiss up a storm.

That’s why the more you can learn to distinguish between calm, anxious and aggressive dog behavior in the moment, the better prepared you’ll be to avoid an impending disaster.

“Dogs talk all the time. They're trying to talk to us the same way we talk to each other,” says veterinary behaviorist Dr. Shana Gilbert-Gregory. “The problem is we don't understand them. They're not capable of learning our language, so we have to learn theirs.”1

Examples of Relaxed, Anxious, and Aggressive Body Language

To understand a dog’s communication signals, it’s necessary to pay attention to specific body postures, movements, and facial gestures. Gilbert-Gregory offers some clues:

How a dog looks when relaxed:

  • Posture — The weight is carried evenly; may do a play bow or wiggle
  • Tail — Relaxed and neutral position; may be wagging
  • Ears — Neutral position
  • Mouth — May be open with tongue hanging out, or may be closed with lips relaxed over teeth
  • Eyes — Soft, with normal pupil size
  • Appetite — Readily eats

How a dog looks when anxious:

  • Posture (and fur) — Piloerection (raised hair on the shoulders and back); might roll over and lift a forelimb
  • Mouth — Might show a submissive smile (a very wide smile), or may be panting, lip licking and/or yawning
  • Ears — Pinned back
  • Eyes — Whale eye* (white portion of eye showing at corner or rim), pupil dilation or averted gaze

*A note about whale eye according to Gilbert-Gregory: “The dog is saying, ‘I am not a threat, and I'm not sure if I'm going to need to move away from you to disengage from this situation’. It's a stress signal.”

How a dog looks when aggressive:

  • Posture — Muscles tense, weight shifts back and low to the ground; may also roll over to expose belly or raise one paw
  • Hair — Piloerection is a red flag
  • Tail — May be tucked or low to the ground; may be wagging slowly or rapidly
  • Mouth — Pulled back, with possible growling, snarling, excessive panting, lip licking, chewing or yawning

Gilbert-Gregory makes the excellent point that aggression is actually a normal, natural form of communication for dogs. If they perceive a threat, they prepare to protect themselves. However, the way humans respond to a dog’s aggression is also normal because it’s scary, especially when it’s unexpected.

Aggressive dogs can also be frightening for veterinary staff. “When you walk into an exam room and the dog is yawning or lip licking in response to your arrival or approach, they're likely politely telling you to back up and disengage,” says Gilbert-Gregory.

10 Signs of a Happy Dog

  1. His eyes and eyelids are relaxed, he blinks a lot, his gaze is soft, and his brow is smooth. His ears are also relaxed, not cocked or pointing. His mouth is open a bit with a few teeth visible (but not bared), his tongue may be lolling, and he may even appear to be smiling.
  2. She’s holding her body in a relaxed posture vs. a tense or stiff stance. She’s holding her tail high and wagging it with such gusto her whole body is wiggling. Alternatively, her tail may be in a more neutral position, with a softer, slower wag.
  3. He has no destructive behaviors, even when he’s home alone. Happy dogs generally get plenty of physical and mental stimulation. Bored, under-exercised, under-stimulated dogs are more likely to become destructive, along with dogs who suffer from separation anxiety.
  4. She loves to play. Happy dogs are always up for a game or a walk or a ride in the car. Since exercise and play are so natural for dogs, if your canine companion doesn’t seem interested, she may be dealing with some pain or an illness, and it’s time to make an appointment with your veterinarian.
  5. He’s belly-up and tongue out. Happy dogs tend to show their bellies and tongues as they wriggle around on their backs. Happy belly displays are different from submissive belly rolls in which the dog’s mouth is usually closed and his body is stiff.
  6. Her appetite is good, which indicates she’s both happy and feeling physically well. A noticeable change in your pet's appetite can be a symptom of an underlying condition. 
  7. He’s happy barking. Some dogs rarely bark, but those who do tend to have a higher-pitched bark when they’re happy that usually doesn’t last long.
  8. She play bows. Many happy dogs raise their backsides in the air and lower their chests to the ground as an invitation to play with either their favorite human or a doggy friend.
  9. He leans into you. A happy dog will often lean into your hand when you pet him and lean into or keep contact with your body whenever the opportunity presents itself.

She’s thrilled to see you. Happy dogs are without fail excited to see their human come through the door, even if said human has only stepped outside for a minute to check the weather!

Sources and References

  • dvm360, November 9, 2019

item.title: When Your 4-Legged Friend Gets the Shakes
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Hypoglycemia, or low blood sugar, happens when a dog's body burns through glucose faster than it can produce it, starving the body’s cells of essential fuel
  • Warning signs range from subtle to severe: trembling, weakness, poor coordination, confusion, twitching, vision loss, or seizures. Mild symptoms can escalate into a crisis within minutes
  • Puppies, toy breeds, diabetic dogs, working or hunting dogs, and pets with liver disease, Addison's, or pancreatic tumors face the highest risk of sudden, unexpected blood sugar crashes
  • Rubbing honey, maple syrup, or corn syrup onto the gums, keeping your dog warm, and calling the vet immediately is the standard emergency response for any suspected hypoglycemic episode
  • Xylitol, a sweetener found in sugar-free gum, peanut butter, mints, and baked goods, is extremely toxic to dogs and can trigger dangerous hypoglycemia or acute liver failure at surprisingly small doses

One minute your dog is trotting around the kitchen looking for a snack. The next, they're standing oddly still, legs trembling, eyes a little glazed, not quite themselves. Or maybe they collapse mid-play, or seem confused about which direction the front door is. It's the kind of moment that flips your stomach because you know something isn't right, but you don't yet know what.

One possibility worth understanding is hypoglycemia (low blood sugar). It's rare, but when it happens, it can move fast, and knowing what to look for and what to do first can make the difference between a quick recovery at home and an emergency trip to the vet.

What Low Blood Sugar Actually Is

Glucose is the main fuel your dog's body runs on, especially their brain. When circulating blood sugar drops below the normal range, cells, especially brain cells, ) start running short on the energy they need to function. That's what produces the shakiness, weakness, confusion, and, in serious cases, seizures or loss of consciousness.

Blood sugar drops happen for one of three basic reasons: your dog's body uses glucose faster than it can produce it, doesn't produce enough to begin with, or produces too much insulin, which pulls glucose out of circulation. Any of these can send levels crashing — sometimes within minutes.1

The Signs You're Watching For

Symptoms can be subtle at first and escalate quickly. Some dogs give only a hint that something's off before dropping into more obvious trouble, while others go from fine to visibly weak within minutes. Common signs include:

  • Trembling or shaking
  • Weakness or unusual lethargy
  • Wobbly walking or lack of coordination
  • Confusion or disorientation
  • Muscle twitching
  • Loss of appetite
  • Vomiting or diarrhea
  • Vision changes or apparent blindness
  • Seizures
  • Collapse or loss of consciousness

Every one of these warrants attention, even if it seems mild. Hypoglycemia can worsen rapidly, and mild wobbliness can turn into a seizure or unconsciousness within a short window if blood sugar keeps dropping.2

Who's Most at Risk

Some dogs are more prone to blood sugar crashes than others. The higher-risk groups include:3,4

  • Puppies under 3 months old: their systems don't yet regulate glucose well
  • Toy breeds: Chihuahuas, Yorkshire Terriers, Pomeranians, Maltese, Toy Poodles, Papillons, Shih Tzus, Pekingese, and Miniature Pinschers all tend to have smaller livers and less glucose reserve
  • Dogs with diabetes: especially those on insulin
  • Hunting, working, and highly active dogs: hypoglycemia can occur during intense exertion ("hunting dog hypoglycemia")
  • Dogs with liver disease, Addison's disease, pancreatic tumors (insulinomas), or portosystemic shunts
  • Dogs recovering from severe infection or sepsis

If your dog fits one of these categories, staying extra alert to symptoms — and having a plan for what to do — is worth it.

What Causes It

The causes stretch from routine to serious. Missed meals or a longer-than-usual gap between feedings can trigger a drop, especially in puppies and small breeds. Intense exercise on an empty stomach can do the same in a working or hunting dog. Diabetic dogs can drop dangerously low if insulin doses and food don't line up correctly. Then there are more concerning causes, such as:5,6

  • Insulinomas (tumors of the pancreas) produce excess insulin and can drop blood sugar without warning. Liver disease disrupts the organ's ability to store and release glucose, which is one of the liver's most important background jobs.
  • Addison's disease interferes with hormones that keep blood sugar stable, and about a quarter of dogs with Addison's show hypoglycemia at some point.

item.title: What You Need to Know if Your Dog Starts Choking
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Fortunately, dogs don't choke very often, but when they do it can quickly escalate to a life-threatening emergency
  • In a pet choking emergency: remain calm, check your dog's mouth for a foreign object, and remove it if you can do so without injuring yourself or your pet
  • If you can't remove the object, perform the Heimlich maneuver to attempt to dislodge it
  • When the object is dislodged, check your dog's airway, breathing and heart rate, perform CPR if necessary, and get your pet to your veterinarian or an emergency animal hospital immediately
  • Never pull on string or cord hanging from the mouth, and don’t try to remove sharp objects or deeply lodged bones at home, as these require immediate veterinary care

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published February 17, 2019.

Most dogs are indiscriminate eaters who also like to chew things they shouldn't. This combination is a set-up for potential disaster, as any experienced dog parent can attest. No matter how tiny a dog is, or how old, or how well-trained, most swallow (or try to swallow) something they shouldn’t at least once in their lives.

The most common cause of choking in dogs is ingestion of an object that lodges in the airway, including things like hard rubber balls, broken pieces of toys, and chew sticks that swell when they become moist.

It can sometimes be difficult to tell whether a dog is choking or just coughing. The difference is that a choking dog will be struggling to breathe, whereas a dog who is just coughing will breathe relatively normally. If your dog is choking, he's actually suffocating, and he’ll get panicky. Also watch for pawing at the mouth.

Fortunately, it's uncommon for pets to choke, especially to the point of unconsciousness, but if your dog ever does, you should be prepared to take lifesaving measures.

First Things First: Remember to Keep Your Cool in a Choking Emergency

Maintaining your composure when faced with a choking emergency can be hard to do, but it’s really important if you want to ensure your furry family member gets the help she needs. If you stay calm, you’ll be better able to provide first aid, as well as vital information to the people treating your pet. In addition, your animal companion can sense your fear, which will raise her stress level and decrease the chance for a good outcome.

In the event of any crisis involving your pet, it’s best to call your veterinarian or a local emergency animal hospital right away (or an animal poison hotline if you think your dog has ingested a poison). However, if the situation is immediately life-threatening, such as a choking incident, taking matters into your own hands may be necessary to save your pet.

Check Your Dog’s Mouth for Foreign Objects

If you can see the object, you can try to remove it — but only if you can do it without injuring yourself or your pet.

Have a helper put one hand on your dog’s upper jaw and the other on the lower, grasp the jaws and press the lips over the teeth so they are between the teeth and the person’s fingers. If you’re working alone, keep the index finger on your lower hand free to sweep the mouth. Any dog can bite when panicked, so use every precaution.

Look inside your dog’s mouth and sweep your finger from the back of the mouth forward to try to remove the obstruction, except in the following situations, which require immediate veterinary intervention:

  • If there are bones lodged deep in your dog’s throat, do not try to pull them out, as this can only be done safely on sedated pets
  • If there is anything hanging from your dog’s mouth (e.g., thread, string, cord, etc.) don’t pull it or cut it, as doing so may cause injury to the throat, esophagus, or other structures
  • If the swallowed object is sharp, don’t try to remove it yourself

In the above situations, or in the event you can’t move the object in your dog’s mouth or throat with your fingers, it’s crucial that you get your dog to your veterinarian or the nearest emergency animal hospital immediately.

How to Perform the Heimlich Maneuver

If your dog is choking and you can’t see anything in her mouth, especially if she’s unconscious, attempt the Heimlich maneuver as follows:

  1. Open her mouth and check for a foreign object. If you can see something in the mouth or throat, try to remove it with your fingers, or grip her tongue and pull it toward you to try to dislodge the object. Alternatively, move your finger around inside your dog's mouth to try to feel and dislodge any foreign object. (There is obviously a risk of being bitten, so take appropriate precautions anytime you put your fingers in your pet's mouth.)
  2. If you have no luck dislodging the object by manually removing it, pick your dog up and place his back against your chest. Put both hands under his waist area behind the ribs. Make a fist with your hands, place them behind the last rib, and rapidly push up and in 5 times.
    • If your dog is too heavy to lift, stand behind him, place your arms around him under the rib cage, make a fist with both hands, and pull in and upward rapidly 5 times.
    • If your dog is unconscious and too heavy to lift, lay him on his right side. Kneel beside him with his legs pointing toward you. Place one hand on the other and place the palm of the bottom hand right behind his ribs. Push in and up 5 times rapidly.
  3. Open your dog's mouth again and look for any foreign object dislodged during the abdominal thrusts you just performed. Move your finger around in his mouth to dislodge and remove the object.
  4. If the object still hasn't been dislodged, with your dog on the ground, put your hands in front of his hips, then lift and suspend him with his head toward the floor.
    • If he's too heavy to lift, lift his back feet until his head is lower than his hips.
  5. Recheck your pet's mouth and use your finger to feel for the object and remove it.
  6. If this doesn't work, put your dog in a sitting or standing position and use the palm of your hand to deliver 5 sharp blows to his back between the shoulder blades.
  7. Open your dog's mouth to check again for a foreign object. You might want to use a small flashlight to get a better look inside. Use your fingers to try to find and clear the object.
  8. Until the object is dislodged, continue to repeat the above steps.
  9. If your dog loses consciousness, give him 5 breaths followed by 5 abdominal thrusts and continue these 2 steps (breaths and thrusts) until the object is dislodged.

As soon as the object is dislodged, check your dog’s airway, breathing and heart rate. Perform CPR if necessary and get your dog to your veterinarian or an emergency animal hospital immediately.

item.title: Could a Little Green Goodness Help Those Beautiful Eyes?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Feeding your pets avocado may actually benefit their health, as long as they eat only the flesh of the fruit. Serving avocado as treats or as an addition to their nutritionally adequate, species-appropriate diet can be good for your pet
  • Avocados contain plenty of healthy fats, with 2.75 grams in every two-tablespoon serving. They also contain antioxidants, particularly lutein and zeaxanthin, which are crucial for optimal eyesight
  • One of the most notable benefits of this fruit is helping boost the bioavailability of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) found in other foods
  • Avocados may also benefit your pet's gut bacteria
  • Avocados' reputation for being poisonous for pets is due to a toxin named persin. However, it's the seed, skin and leaves that contain high amounts of persin. The flesh only contains very minimal amounts that shouldn't be a cause for concern

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published September 6, 2020.

Avocados are one of the trendiest fruits these days. More and more studies are coming out showing that they can benefit human health.1,2 But what about your four-legged pal? Can they benefit from avocados, too? It turns out, they can — and you shouldn't be worried about the claims that these fruits are "poisonous" to pets, with some caveats.

What's more, the majority of avocados sold in the supermarket are free from pesticides, according to a report from the Environmental Working Group (EWG). In fact, avocados rank third at the EWG's "Clean Fifteen" list.3 However, it's still better to purchase organic avocados from certified producers whenever possible. This will help lower your and your pet's exposure to agricultural chemicals whenever avocados are consumed.

Avocado Fun Fact

The Hass avocado is one of the most popular varieties sold around the world, but it originally came about by coincidence. According to Smithsonian Magazine, Rudolph Hass took home some seedlings to graft with other avocado varieties.

One seedling didn't mesh well with his grafts, so he left it to grow on its own. After some time, Rudolph's children noticed that the tree produced "a rich, nutty slightly oily taste." Surprisingly, this variety tasted better than his other experiments — and the Hass avocado was born.4

In one study, researchers experimented on the possible effects of oleic acid in test rats for 14 days. By the end of the study, they noted that oleic acid had hypotensive effects that helped lower blood pressure. Moreover, stability in blood pressure was observed to last for around three to four days.10 Another study found that oleic acid had neuroprotective effects in rats. Researchers attributed this effect to the fatty acid's anti-inflammatory properties.11

Avocados Can Also Give Your Pet Antioxidants

Avocados contain antioxidants, particularly lutein and zeaxanthin, which are crucial for optimal eyesight.12 Research has shown that both lutein and zeaxanthin are concentrated in the retina and their importance for eye health cannot be ignored, as noted in this study in the Journal of Ophthalmology:13

"In these animal models, lutein and zeaxanthin have been reported to have beneficial effects in protecting ocular tissues and cells (especially the retinal neurons) against damage caused by different etiological factors.   • Magnesium (5.43 milligrams) — It acts as a cofactor for various cellular enzymes needed in energy metabolism.

“When feeding avocados to your pet, only give them the fleshy part (the same part you eat), and in small quantities at a time.”

Take care to remove the skin and the pit to ensure that you're not inadvertently poisoning your dog with the high amounts of persin in those parts of the avocado.34

The quality of the avocado is also important. Try purchasing organic avocados from certified producers whenever possible. While avocados belong to EWG's Clean Fifteen list, organically grown varieties can help lower your pet's exposure to chemicals compared to conventionally grown ones, even if they're "clean."

If you have avocado plants growing in your garden, make sure your pets do not ingest the stems, leaves or the tree bark (though this is very unlikely to happen).

On the off chance that your pet consumes the inedible parts of the fruit, you need to be aware of the signs of persin toxicity so that you can get your pet help right away:35

  • Vomiting
  • Diarrhea
  • Respiratory distress
  • Congestion

Treats should comprise less than 10% of your pet's daily caloric intake. If you feed your pet homemade meals, make sure you follow a recipe that's been formulated to meet your pet's minimum nutrient requirements.

item.title: This Quintessential Breed Is Almost Perfect in Every Way
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Schapendoes, a quintessential “shaggy dog” with his ground-sweeping, wavy hair, may look like a disheveled pup, but his coat is easier to take care of than you might think and won’t need to be cut or clipped
  • Also known as the Dutch Sheepdog, the Schapendoes breed was considered an “all-around farm dog” during the 19th and early 20th centuries around his home turf of the Netherlands
  • Naturally athletic and energetic, the Schapendoes has a “springy” and light-footed gait when they run, and one of their most important hallmarks is their amazing jumping ability
  • Being smart, lively, eager to please and easy to train, you can expect your Schapendoes to live a good long life with few problems, and to be a good companion, and fun, for both kids and other pets
  • Daily exercise and mental stimulation are important, since a bored Schapendoes can develop a barking problem

Editor's Note: This article is a reprint. It was originally published November 16, 2017.

Described as cheerful, funny and brave, the Schapendoes breed may look like a mop of a dog with their unruly-looking fur hanging into their eyes, but this Dutch herding dog, also known as the quintessential “shaggy dog,” is actually quite easy to groom.

It’s evident that they sport a dense double coat, but their lightly wavy hair, which can make them look much larger and broader than they are, can touch the ground both on his front and hind legs. Their hair (which couldn’t really be called “fur”) typically reaches 3 inches in length at the longest point, which is at their hindquarters, but it’s fine and doesn’t even require clipping or trimming. The Schapendoes Club notes that:

“The coat, where it is long, is inclined to stand off in tufts, giving the Schapendoes a large girth, especially at the rear. The Schapendoes has a tremendous top knot, moustache and beard.”1

That doesn’t mean this adorable dog doesn’t need checking a few times a week to make sure his fur doesn’t get matted, which it may when they’re puppies until their “adult” coat comes in. It may be hard to believe, but this breed sheds very little, even though VetStreet comments that it’s normal for them to “look a little unkempt.”2

Schapendoes Breed: Origination and Characteristics

This Dutch Sheepdog was considered more than a sheepdog around his original home turf of the northeastern Drenthe province of the Netherlands, as his official title may have been more like “all-around farm dog” during the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Outside this area of the world, this breed was very little known, and in fact wasn’t recognized as a breed unto itself until World War I, when it almost faded from existence. This occurred because in the 1940s, border collies were being imported that began overshadowing the native breed until its own club was formed in 1947, known as the Nederlandse Schapendoes.

In 1954, a breed standard was set forth, complete with a studbook, but they weren’t formally recognized as a Dutch breed until 1971. The Fédération Cynologique Internationale, or World Canine Organization, added the breed to their list in 1989. In the U.S. the Schapendoes breed — which is the singular, not the plural — joined the American Kennel Club, but does not, as yet, enjoy full recognition as a breed.

Close relatives to this breed include bearded collies, the puli, briard, Polish Loweland Sheepdog and the Bergamasco. The Schapendoes is typically a combination of white, gray, brown, black and blue-black, but the Schapendoes Club stresses that while it may tend to be curly, “frizzy hair is not permitted,” and it should never be silky. They also have a lot of hair emerging from between their toes, a long, feathery tail, which, when they jump, serves as a sort of rudder and flies out behind them when they run.

Attributes of the Schapendoes

One of the things that may surprise anyone watching naturally athletic Schapendoes at play is how “springy” and light-footed they are when they run. In fact, one of the most often-mentioned notations of the breed is its amazing jumping ability. You’ll often hear people mention making sure your fences are high enough.

That’s one skill that makes the breed so excellent when it comes to agility training and other competitive sports for dogs. If you have a field or open grasslands where they can safely run unimpeded, they’re very happy, and they’re eager to join you on your run, hike or on the trail on a daily basis.

Afterward, very much like humans, they’re just as happy to join you on the couch, as they’re very people oriented. Schapendoes get along well with children, although a natural tendency to herd might be something to watch for, as they can begin “nudging” people who are shorter than their usual 16- to 20-inch height, and depending on the bulk of their usual 26- to 55-pound weight, this nudge could cause a child to fall. With children under a certain age, they should be closely supervised, as with any other dog.

This breed also plays and lives happily amongst other dogs and even cats, especially if they were raised together. Understandably, there aren’t nearly the number of Schapendoes in the sheepherding business as there once were, so this breed has settled down to become a beloved family dog. But like many other dogs with a long history of activity like this one has, exercise is important.

Schapendoes: Smart, Cooperative and Playful

The Schapendoes Club site mentions their general expression as being “open-minded, honest and lively.” Further:

item.title: What Else Are You Serving at Dinnertime?
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • A 2026 Clean Label Project report tested 79 top-selling dog foods and found dry kibble contained 5.7x more arsenic, 3.2x more cadmium, 2.7x more mercury, and 12.7x more lead than average human food on an as fed basis
  • Compared with fresh or frozen dog foods (on an as fed basis rather than a dry matter basis), dry kibble carried 13x more arsenic, 6x more cadmium, 21x more mercury, and 21x more lead — with the highest single lead reading topping 1,576 parts per billion
  • Meat by-products, vitamin and mineral premixes, and seafood or plant-based carbohydrates like rice appear to be the three main ingredient categories driving heavy metal contamination in dry kibble
  • Heavy metals can accumulate in the liver, kidneys, brain, and nervous system over time, with recent research correlating cadmium exposure to cancer risk in dogs, who face cancer diagnosis rates up to five times higher than humans
  • No comprehensive federal regulations limit dietary exposure to industrial contaminants in dog food — practical fixes include moving away from all-kibble diets, avoiding by-product formulas, and filtering drinking water

You scoop the kibble into the bowl. Your dog does the happy dance. You feel like you have done your one job — putting good food in front of a family member who trusts you completely. But if new independent testing on some of the most popular dog foods on the shelf is any indication, that bowl of dinner may contain some ingredients that never made it onto the label.

A report published in 2026 by the nonprofit Clean Label Project tested 79 top-selling dog food products for heavy metals, bisphenols, phthalates, acrylamide, glyphosate, and other industrial contaminants. What they found should give any pet parent pause — especially those feeding conventional dry kibble every day for years on end.1,2

What the Testing Actually Found

The Clean Label Project analyzed 50 dry dog food products, 11 air-dried or freeze-dried, and 18 fresh or frozen — running more than 11,376 individual contaminant tests through an ISO-accredited chemistry laboratory. The organization then compared the results to a benchmark drawn from over 3,280 human food, beverage, and supplement products they had previously tested. On average, dry dog food contained:3

  • 5.7 times more arsenic than human food averages
  • 3.2 times more cadmium
  • 2.7 times more mercury
  • 12.7 times more lead

Compared with fresh or frozen dog foods on an as fed basis, the numbers were even more striking. Dry kibble carried 13.3 times more arsenic, 6.1 times more cadmium, 20.7 times more mercury, and 21.2 times more lead than the fresh/frozen samples. Air-dried and freeze-dried options landed in second place — better than kibble, worse than fresh. For clarity, though, this study did not evaluate and compare the various diets on a dry weight basis, which does skew the data and make interpretation more difficult. This study also did not compare ingredient to ingredient across dry kibble, freeze dried, and fresh or frozen diets. Diets containing fish, for instance, will inherently have higher heavy metal levels than land-based protein, so this needs to be considered.

The highest single lead reading in a dry dog food sample was 1,576.5 parts per billion. For context, that is roughly 110 times the average lead level found in the average human food benchmark. And roughly 85% of dog owners feed dry kibble as their pet's primary diet.

Where the Contamination Comes From

Three main ingredient categories seem to drive most of the contamination in dry pet food, according to the Clean Label Project analysis:

  • Meat by-products — This is the catch-all category for the parts of an animal left over after cuts intended for humans are removed — livers, lungs, kidneys, spleens, bones, and other tissues. These get processed into meat by-product meal that shows up in a lot of dry kibble. The problem is that heavy metals concentrate specifically in the organs and bones where the body filters and stores them. So when you make meal from those parts, you are also concentrating the metals.
  • Vitamin and mineral premixes — Nearly every commercial pet food adds a synthetic vitamin and mineral premix to hit the nutritional labels required by regulators. Those premixes can naturally contain trace metals, and factors like country of origin, supply chain complexity, and inspection practices affect how much ends up in the final product. When ingredients change hands through multiple international suppliers, traceability breaks down.
  • Seafood and plant-based carbohydrates — Fish carry mercury and long-chain contaminants they have bioaccumulated from ocean and freshwater food webs. Grains and root vegetables can pull arsenic and cadmium out of the soil they are grown in — rice, in particular, is a well-known arsenic sponge.

Each of these on its own might contribute only a small amount. But dry kibble typically combines all three, and the cumulative effect on the finished product is measurable — and consistent enough to show up across major brands. Add in high-heat processing (which produces acrylamide, another contaminant found at elevated levels in dry kibble) and packaging materials that can leach phthalates like DEHP, and you have a product that looks like food but reads chemically like something else.

Not Just the Bowl

Heavy metal exposure for pets does not stop at the food bowl. Veterinary toxicologists see a range of metal-related concerns from household and environmental sources as well. According to Dr. Christine Rutter at Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine, the most common metal intoxication showing up in emergency vet visits is actually zinc — usually from a dog swallowing a penny.4

Pennies minted after 1982 are copper-coated zinc discs. Once the stomach acid strips off the copper, the zinc irritates the GI tract and gets absorbed into the bloodstream, where it can destabilize red blood cells and cause them to rupture. Other zinc sources to keep away from pets include wire crate bars they might chew, diaper creams, and zinc-based sunscreens they can lick off skin.

Lead exposure in pets often comes from ingesting paint chips from older homes (leaded paint was banned in the U.S. in 1978 but is still present in older homes and antique toys), painted objects, fishing lures, or ammunition fragments. Copper can build up in certain breeds — Labs, West Highland white terriers, cocker spaniels, and Doberman pinschers — that carry a genetic predisposition to copper storage disorders.5

What Long-Term Exposure Actually Does

Heavy metals build up over time. They accumulate primarily in the liver and kidneys — the organs responsible for filtering them out — but they also reach the brain and nervous system. Recent scientific research has linked increased exposure to cadmium with cancer in pets and to heavy metals overall with increased mortality. And dogs, notably, have a cancer rate equal to and up to 5 times that of humans (depending on breed).6

There are many reasons for the dog cancer rate — genetics, spay/neuter status, sex, exercise, environmental exposures — but diet is on the list. If your dog eats the same processed food every day for years, and that food carries chronic low-dose heavy metal contamination, the cumulative exposure over a lifetime is significant.

The Morris Animal Foundation is currently funding a multi-year study out of the University of Wisconsin — Madison specifically looking at toxic heavy metal burden in aging dogs. Human research has already tied heavy metal accumulation to Alzheimer's disease, other dementias, hearing loss, and vision loss. Researchers are now tracking whether the same relationships hold up in aging dogs — with one arm of the study focused on dogs living in Flint and Detroit, cities famously known for lead in their water.7

The early results are still coming in, but a related publication in the journal PLoS One in 2024 already documented meaningful dual sensory impairments (both hearing and vision) in senior companion dogs and their relationship to cognitive decline. It is a research area worth watching.8

The Regulatory Gap

Here is the uncomfortable part: There are no comprehensive federal regulations that specifically limit dietary exposure to industrial and environmental contaminants in dog food. Most current safety oversight focuses on things like physical contaminants (bone fragments, packaging pieces) and microbiological hazards (salmonella, listeria). Heavy metals, bisphenols, phthalates, glyphosate, and acrylamide levels are not federally capped in pet food the way they are in human food, and even in human food, some of these limits are still under active debate.

This is why independent testing organizations like the Clean Label Project have stepped in — because the market is not currently set up to hold manufacturers accountable for what ends up in the bag. As long as the labels meet Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) nutritional standards, there is very little else being systematically checked.

Nutritional adequacy — meaning the food contains the right protein, fat, and vitamin percentages — is a very different question from whether the food is free of industrial pollutants. A product can technically be complete and balanced by the numbers on the guaranteed analysis and still carry a contamination profile no one is testing for.

What You Can Actually Do

This is not about panic. It is about being thoughtful with a daily decision that adds up over your pet's lifetime. Practical steps that make a real difference:

  • Move away from all-kibble diets when possible — Fresh and frozen dog foods came in dramatically lower in contaminants across the Clean Label Project testing when evaluating on an as fed basis. If a full fresh diet is not feasible, consider mixing fresh in with kibble to reduce cumulative exposure.
  • Avoid meat by-product-heavy formulas — Look at the ingredient list. If the top ingredients include "meat by-products" or "meat by-product meal," that is the ingredient category most associated with concentrated heavy metals. Whole named meats (chicken, beef, turkey) rather than generic by-products are a step in a better direction.
  • Rotate proteins and skip long-term fish-heavy diets — Fish-based foods carry mercury and long-chain PFAS. Rotating land-based proteins reduces exposure.
  • Choose brands that publish testing — A few pet food companies now voluntarily test for and disclose contaminant results. That transparency is worth rewarding.
  • Filter your pet's drinking water — Standard carbon filters do not remove heavy metals. Look for a high-quality filtration system designed to remove heavy metals and other contaminants.
  • Watch what your dog gets into around the house — Keep pennies, old paint, fishing tackle, ammunition, diaper cream, and zinc sunscreens out of reach. Chewers should stay away from powder-coated or galvanized wire crates.
  • Consider your local environment — If you live in an older home, in an area with known lead contamination, or near industrial sites, that factors into your dog's cumulative load. Home lead testing kits for paint and surfaces are widely available and inexpensive.
  • Support detoxification — Talk to an integrative or holistic veterinarian about diet strategies that support your pet's natural detoxification pathways — good hydration, quality protein, antioxidant-rich fresh whole foods, and periodic nutritional support for liver and kidney function.

The Bigger Picture

The Clean Label Project's report puts numbers on something integrative and holistic veterinarians have been warning about for years — that the modern commercial pet food supply is not the neutral, harmless product the packaging suggests. It is a heavily processed, globally sourced product with limited regulatory oversight and measurable industrial contamination baked in.

None of this means your dog's next bowl of kibble is going to send them to the vet. The concern is chronic, cumulative, low-dose exposure across the 10 to 15 years your pet is with you. That is the timeline over which heavy metals accumulate in organs, tissue damage builds, and the body's ability to compensate wears down.

Your pet does not get to read the ingredient panel. They rely on you to be the person who does. The good news is that the choices that reduce their contamination load are the same ones that generally improve their overall diet — more fresh whole foods, less ultra-processed content, better ingredient sourcing, filtered water, and awareness of what they are being exposed to in the home. Small changes to what goes in the bowl every day, added up over a lifetime, actually move the needle.

What else are you serving at dinnertime? That is a question worth asking. And thanks to independent testing groups pushing the industry toward more transparency, it is a question you can increasingly find honest answers to.

Sources and References

  • 1 Clean Label Project, February 12, 2026
  • 2,3,6 CLP Insights: Extremely High Levels of Lead, Mercury, Arsenic, and Cadmium Found in Dry Dog Food, February 12, 2026
  • 4,5 Texas A&M University Veterinary Medicine & Biomedical Sciences March 19, 2026
  • 7 Morris Animal Foundation, Understanding Toxic Heavy Metal Burden in Aging Dogs
  • 8 PLoS One, October 16, 2024

The Clean Label Project's report puts numbers on something integrative and holistic veterinarians have been warning about for years — that the modern commercial pet food supply is not the neutral, harmless product the packaging suggests. It is a heavily processed, globally sourced product with limited regulatory oversight and measurable industrial contamination baked in.

That is the timeline over which heavy metals accumulate in organs, tissue damage builds, and the body's ability to compensate wears down.

Your pet does not get to read the ingredient panel. They rely on you to be the person who does. Small changes to what goes in the bowl every day, added up over a lifetime, actually move the needle.

item.title: Tea Time Is Not Just for Two-Legged Family Members
item.description:
STORY AT-A-GLANCE

  • Green tea comes from the Camellia sinensis plant and is packed with polyphenol compounds called catechins — especially EGCG, the most studied and potent one behind most of green tea's health effects
  • Integrative veterinarians point to EGCG's antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular, cognitive, and cancer-supportive properties, with research showing it may complement chemotherapy and reduce certain treatment side effects
  • Brewed tea alone does not reach therapeutic levels — you would need about ten cups a day for a human — which is why properly (ie veterinary) formulated green tea extracts or polyphenol blends are usually the better delivery option for pets
  • Only use organic, water-decaffeinated green tea for pets. Caffeine is toxic to dogs and cats, and chemical decaffeination methods can leave residues and strip beneficial polyphenols
  • Skip green tea for pets with liver disease, kidney disease, ulcers, glaucoma, high blood pressure, or those pregnant, nursing, or very young — and always start with small amounts under guidance from an integrative vet

Somewhere between the second sip of your morning cup of green tea and the moment your dog rests their chin on your knee, you might have wondered: Is there anything in this warm, earthy drink that could actually help them, too? It is a fair question. And it turns out the answer, according to a growing number of integrative veterinarians, is more interesting than you might expect.

Green tea has been the subject of thousands of studies in humans. What is newer is how much attention it is getting in the veterinary world, particularly among vets who focus on natural and complementary approaches to chronic disease. The plant compounds in those little dried leaves are turning out to have effects on inflammation, oxidative stress, and even certain cancer pathways — with promising implications for the four-legged members of your family.

What Green Tea Actually Is

Green tea and black tea both come from the Camellia sinensis plant, but what separates them is how the leaves are processed. To make green tea, the leaves are steamed or pan-fried quickly after harvest, which stops oxidation and keeps them green. Black tea is allowed to oxidize before drying, which changes the color and the chemistry, generating different compounds like theaflavins and tannins.1,2

Green tea leaves are packed with plant compounds called polyphenols, along with vitamins, minerals, and amino acids. The main polyphenols in green tea are a group called catechins, and the star of the group is a mouthful of a name: epigallocatechin gallate, or EGCG. This one compound is behind most of what the research talks about when it comes to green tea's health effects.3,4

Why Integrative Vets Are Paying Attention

For years, holistic and integrative veterinarians have looked for natural tools that can support their patients through everything from arthritis to cancer to cognitive decline. Green tea keeps coming up in the conversation because EGCG appears to work on several fronts at once.5,6,7

  • Antioxidant activity — Oxidative stress, the imbalance between free radicals and the body's antioxidant defenses, has been linked to a long list of chronic conditions in pets, including cancer, heart disease, and neurodegenerative disorders. EGCG is one of the most studied natural antioxidants out there, with a solid track record of neutralizing free radicals and reducing oxidative damage in cells.
  • Anti-inflammatory effects — Chronic inflammation shows up in almost every long-term veterinary condition, from arthritis to inflammatory bowel disease to skin issues. Studies point to EGCG's ability to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines and modulate inflammatory signaling pathways, which may help take the edge off chronic conditions in pets that live with them long-term.
  • Cardiovascular support — Heart disease is a common concern in older dogs, especially certain small breeds. Research in rats and mice suggests EGCG may support healthy blood pressure, improve the function of the endothelial lining of blood vessels, and help maintain healthy heart muscle contractility — modest but meaningful contributions to cardiovascular health in aging pets.
  • Cancer support — This is where green tea has drawn the most attention. Cancer remains a leading cause of death in dogs and one of the biggest worries for pet parents. EGCG has been shown to interfere with several of the pathways cancer cells use to grow — including triggering apoptosis (programmed cell death), inhibiting angiogenesis (the new blood vessels tumors need to expand), and interfering with VEGF, a signaling molecule cancers depend on. EGCG also inhibits receptor tyrosine kinase activity, which is the same target class as some newer chemotherapy drugs like Palladia.

    Interestingly, when used alongside conventional chemotherapy, EGCG has been shown in research to complement — not interfere with — treatment. It may reduce chemo side effects, help chemo work more effectively by inhibiting a resistance mechanism called P-glycoprotein, and even reduce the risk of secondary tumors that certain chemotherapy drugs can trigger. This is why some integrative oncology veterinarians consider it as an adjunct in complex cancer cases.
  • Cognitive support — Cognitive dysfunction syndrome — sometimes called doggy dementia or feline cognitive decline — is one of the harder things to watch in aging pets. EGCG has been shown to help reduce beta-amyloid plaques (the same abnormal protein buildups seen in human Alzheimer's disease) and may support cognitive function in senior animals. It is not a cure, but it is part of a broader nutritional strategy that many integrative veterinarians are using with older patients.

Brewed Tea vs. Supplement Form

Here is where practical reality catches up with the research. The bioavailability of EGCG when you simply drink brewed green tea is actually pretty poor. To hit anything like a therapeutic dose through the tea itself, a human would need to drink around 10 cups a day — which is a lot even for the most dedicated tea drinker, and simply impractical for a dog or cat. This is why integrative veterinarians typically reach for a properly formulated green tea extract or a broader polyphenol blend rather than trying to work with brewed tea alone.8 Concentrated green tea extracts, though, do have an increased risk of liver toxicity in cats and dogs. Be sure to consult your veterinarian regarding dosing prior to giving any concentrated formulations.

That said, small amounts of brewed decaffeinated green tea can still be a nice gentle addition to a pet's routine for antioxidant support, hot spot rinses, or ear wipes. Just don't mistake it for a substitute for a properly dosed supplement when you are dealing with a specific health concern.

The Caffeine Question

Caffeine is toxic to dogs and cats. An 8-ounce cup of green tea contains between 30 and 50 milligrams of caffeine — less than coffee, but still enough to be concerning depending on the size of the pet and the amount consumed. This is why anyone giving green tea to a pet should stick to decaffeinated versions.

How the tea gets decaffeinated matters, too. Chemical solvent-based decaffeination can strip out some of the beneficial polyphenols and leave chemical residues behind. Water-based decaffeination methods (sometimes called Swiss water process) preserve more of the compounds you want and do not leave behind anything you do not. When shopping, look for organic, water-decaffeinated products, and do not be shy about calling the manufacturer to ask how their extract is processed.9

Practical Ways to Use It

If your veterinarian gives you the green light, green tea can be introduced gently and in small amounts. Some approaches integrative vets and pet health writers commonly suggest:10,11

  • Internal use for antioxidant support — Steep organic decaffeinated green tea in water, cool it, and mix a small amount into your dog's food a couple of times a week. Suggested working-up amounts: 1 to 2 tablespoons for small dogs, 1/8 cup for medium dogs, and 1/4 cup for large dogs — but always start smaller and see how your dog responds.
  • As part of a polyphenol supplement blend — For more targeted support (immune, cardiovascular, cognitive, or oncology adjunct), a professional-grade green tea extract or polyphenol formulation from a trusted veterinary supplement brand is usually a better tool than brewed tea.
  • Externally for hot spots and skin irritation — A cool tea bag pressed to an irritated patch of skin — or brewed tea in a spray bottle applied to hot spots — can be soothing thanks to green tea's cooling and anti-inflammatory properties.
  • For dirty ears — Brewed and cooled green tea can be used on a soft cloth or cotton pad to wipe out the outer parts of your dog's ears.
  • Substitute for water — Use it in homemade treat recipes for a mild antioxidant boost.

Cats can technically have small amounts of the same tea, but cats are more sensitive to plant compounds than dogs and require more careful veterinary guidance.

When To Be Cautious

Green tea has one of the safest track records of any natural supplement, but a few situations warrant extra caution. Talk to your integrative veterinarian first if your pet has liver disease, kidney disease, stomach or intestinal ulcers, glaucoma, or high blood pressure. The same conditions that raise flags for humans drinking green tea deserve the same care in pets. Pregnant or nursing pets, and very young puppies and kittens, are also not the right candidates.

If your dog is already on medications or other supplements, check for interactions. And as always, if you see any digestive upset — usually loose stool or a bit of vomiting — that is the signal to lower the amount or stop and check in with your vet.

The Bigger Takeaway

The natural world keeps offering pet parents useful tools, and green tea is one of the better-studied ones out there. Its polyphenols — especially EGCG — bring real, research-backed antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular, cognitive, and even cancer-supportive effects to the table. It is not a cure-all, and it is not a substitute for a good veterinary workup. But for many pets, especially those dealing with chronic inflammation, cognitive changes, or ongoing cancer support, a properly chosen green tea extract can be a genuinely helpful piece of a broader plan.

Talk to an integrative or holistic veterinarian who understands supplements and dosing. Look for high-quality, organic, water-decaffeinated products. Start low, go slow, and pay attention to how your pet responds. Tea time, it turns out, might just be a family affair after all.

Sources and References

  • 1,7,9,11 Adored Beast, July 31, 2023
  • 2,4,6,8,10 Paw and Claws Animal Hospital, Green Tea for Dogs
  • 3,5 Innovative Veterinary Care, July 26, 2024
